q-161793.name: Question 1
q-161793.problem:
Find the Jacobian determinant of the transformation $T,$ defined as

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v \\ w\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}u{e}^{w} \\ w-u \\ w{e}^{u}-3v\end{aligned}].
$$
q-161793.worked_solution:
For a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v \\ w\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have 

$$
x(u,v,w)=u{e}^{w},\,y(u,v,w)=w-u,\,z(u,v,w)=w{e}^{u}-3v.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & ={e}^{w} & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =0 & \,\frac{∂x}{∂w} & =u{e}^{w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =-1 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =0 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂w} & =1 \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & =w{e}^{u} & \,\frac{∂z}{∂v} & =-3, & \,\frac{∂z}{∂w} & ={e}^{u}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =|\begin{aligned}{e}^{w} & 0 & u{e}^{w} \\ -1 & 0 & 1 \\ w{e}^{u} & -3 & {e}^{u}\end{aligned}| \\  & =(-3)(-1)^{3+2}|\begin{aligned}{e}^{w} & u{e}^{w} \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =3({e}^{w}+u{e}^{w}) \\  & =3{e}^{w}(1+u).\end{aligned}
$$

q-161795.name: Question 2
q-161795.problem:
Find the Jacobian determinant of the transformation $T,$ defined as

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v \\ w\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}u+\operatorname{cos}⁡w \\ v \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡u+w\end{aligned}].
$$
q-161795.worked_solution:
For a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v \\ w\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have 

$$
x(u,v,w)=u+\operatorname{cos}⁡w,\,y(u,v,w)=v,\,z(u,v,w)=\operatorname{cos}⁡u+w.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =1 & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =0 & \,\frac{∂x}{∂w} & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡w \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =0 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =1 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂w} & =0 \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡u & \,\frac{∂z}{∂v} & =0, & \,\frac{∂z}{∂w} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -\operatorname{sin}⁡w \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡u & 0 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =1(-1)^{2+2}|\begin{aligned}1 & -\operatorname{sin}⁡w \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡u & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =1-\operatorname{sin}⁡u\,\operatorname{sin}⁡w.\end{aligned}
$$

q-39710.name: Question 3
q-39710.problem:
Find the Jacobian determinant of the transformation $T$ that maps the $uvw$-space into the $xyz$-space by means of the equations

$$
x={u}^{2}+vw,\,y=2-uv,\,z={v}^{2}-w.
$$
q-39710.worked_solution:
For a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v \\ w\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =2u & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =w & \,\frac{∂x}{∂w} & =v \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =-v & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =-u & \,\frac{∂y}{∂w} & =0 \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & =0 & \,\frac{∂z}{∂v} & =2v & \,\frac{∂z}{∂w} & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =|\begin{aligned}2u & w & v \\ -v & -u & 0 \\ 0 & 2v & -1\end{aligned}| \\  & =2u(-1)^{1+1}|\begin{aligned}-u & 0 \\ 2v & -1\end{aligned}|+(-v)(-1)^{2+1}|\begin{aligned}w & v \\ 2v & -1\end{aligned}| \\  & =2u(u-0)+v(-w-2{v}^{2}) \\  & =2{u}^{2}-2{v}^{3}-vw.\end{aligned}

q-161799.name: Question 4
q-161799.problem:
Find the Jacobian determinant of the transformation $T,$ defined as

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v \\ w\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}u+v\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +w\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ 3v \\ u\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +w\end{aligned}].
$$

You may assume that $\theta $ is a fixed constant.
q-161799.worked_solution:
For a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v \\ w\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have 

$$
x(u,v,w)=u+v\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +w\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,y(u,v,w)=3v,\,z(u,v,w)=u\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +w.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =1 & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & \,\frac{∂x}{∂w} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =0 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =3 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂w} & =0 \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & \,\frac{∂z}{∂v} & =0, & \,\frac{∂z}{∂w} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =|\begin{aligned}1 & \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ 0 & 3 & 0 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & 0 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =3(-1)^{2+2}|\begin{aligned}1 & \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =3(1-{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) \\  & =3{cos}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

q-161796.name: Question 5
q-161796.problem:
Find the Jacobian determinant of the transformation $T,$ defined as

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v \\ w\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡(u\,v\,w) \\ u+2w \\ uv\end{aligned}].
$$
q-161796.worked_solution:
For a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v \\ w\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have 

$$
x(u,v,w)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(u\,v\,w),\,y(u,v,w)=u+2w,\,z(u,v,w)=uv.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =\frac{1}{u} & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =\frac{1}{v} & \,\frac{∂x}{∂w} & =\frac{1}{w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =1 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =0 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂w} & =2 \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & =v & \,\frac{∂z}{∂v} & =u & \,\frac{∂z}{∂w} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{u} & \frac{1}{v} & \frac{1}{w} \\ 1 & 0 & 2 \\ v & u & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =\frac{1}{w}(-1)^{1+3}|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ v & u\end{aligned}|+2(-1)^{2+3}|\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{u} & \frac{1}{v} \\ v & u\end{aligned}| \\  & =\frac{1}{w}(u-0)-2(1-1) \\  & =\frac{u}{w}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-39709.name: Question 6
q-39709.problem:
Find the locations of all of the critical points of the transformation $T,$ where $T$ is defined as

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v \\ w\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}{u}^{2}-v \\ {u}^{2}+v \\ {e}^{w}\end{aligned}].
$$
q-39709.worked_solution:
For a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v \\ w\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have 

$$
x(u,v,w)={u}^{2}-v,\,y(u,v,w)={u}^{2}+v,\,z(u,v,w)={e}^{w}.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =2u & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =-1 & \,\frac{∂x}{∂w} & =0 \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =2u & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =1 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂w} & =0 \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & =0 & \,\frac{∂z}{∂v} & =0 & \,\frac{∂z}{∂w} & ={e}^{w}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =|\begin{aligned}2u & -1 & 0 \\ 2u & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & {e}^{w}\end{aligned}| \\  & ={e}^{w}|\begin{aligned}2u & -1 \\ 2u & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & ={e}^{w}(2u+2u) \\  & =4u{e}^{w}.\end{aligned}
$$

The function has critical points when $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}=0.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =0 \\ 4u{e}^{w} & =0 \\ u & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The equation $u=0$ defines the plane $u=0,$ i.e., $vw$-plane.

q-161810.name: Question 7
q-161810.problem:
Find the locations of all of the critical points of the transformation $T,$ where $T$ is defined as

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v \\ w\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}u+vw \\ {v}^{2} \\ w+v\end{aligned}].
$$
q-161810.worked_solution:
For a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v \\ w\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have 

$$
x(u,v,w)=u+vw,\,y(u,v,w)={v}^{2},\,z(u,v,w)=w+v.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =1 & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =w & \,\frac{∂x}{∂w} & =v \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =0 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =2v & \,\frac{∂y}{∂w} & =0 \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & =0 & \,\frac{∂z}{∂v} & =1 & \,\frac{∂z}{∂w} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =|\begin{aligned}1 & w & v \\ 0 & 2v & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =1|\begin{aligned}2v & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =1(2v-0) \\  & =2v.\end{aligned}
$$

The function has critical points when $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}=0.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =0 \\ 2v & =0 \\ v & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The equation $v=0$ defines the plane $v=0,$ i.e., $uw$-plane.

q-161816.name: Question 8
q-161816.problem:
Find the locations of all of the critical points of the transformation $T,$ where $T$ is defined as

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v \\ w\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}{e}^{u} \\ {e}^{u+w} \\ uv+w\end{aligned}].
$$
q-161816.worked_solution:
For a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v \\ w\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have 

$$
x(u,v,w)={e}^{u},\,y(u,v,w)={e}^{u+w},\,z(u,v,w)=uv+w.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & ={e}^{u} & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =0 & \,\frac{∂x}{∂w} & =0 \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & ={e}^{u+w} & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =0 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂w} & ={e}^{u+w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & =v & \,\frac{∂z}{∂v} & =u & \,\frac{∂z}{∂w} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =|\begin{aligned}{e}^{u} & 0 & 0 \\ {e}^{u+w} & 0 & {e}^{u+w} \\ v & u & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & ={e}^{u}|\begin{aligned}0 & {e}^{u+w} \\ u & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & ={e}^{u}(0-u{e}^{u+w}) \\  & =-u{e}^{2u+w}.\end{aligned}
$$

The function has critical points when $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}=0.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =0 \\ -u{e}^{2u+w} & =0 \\ u & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The equation $u=0$ defines the plane $u=0,$ i.e., $vw$-plane.

q-161815.name: Question 9
q-161815.problem:
Find the locations of all of the critical points of the transformation $T,$ where $T$ is defined as

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v \\ w\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}\sqrt{u} \\ vw \\ u+w\end{aligned}].
$$
q-161815.worked_solution:
For a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v \\ w\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have 

$$
x(u,v,w)=\sqrt{u},\,y(u,v,w)=vw,\,z(u,v,w)=u+w.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{u}} & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =0 & \,\frac{∂x}{∂w} & =0 \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =0 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =w & \,\frac{∂y}{∂w} & =v \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & =1 & \,\frac{∂z}{∂v} & =0 & \,\frac{∂z}{∂w} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2\sqrt{u}} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & w & v \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{u}}|\begin{aligned}w & v \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}|+1|\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ w & v\end{aligned}| \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{u}}(w-0)+0 \\  & =\frac{w}{2\sqrt{u}}.\end{aligned}
$$

The function has critical points when $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}=0.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =0 \\ \frac{w}{2\sqrt{u}} & =0 \\ w & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The equation $w=0$ defines the plane $w=0,$ i.e., $uv$-plane.

q-161815.html:
Question 9
?

Find the locations of all of the critical points of the transformation T, where T is defined as

T:[uvw]⟶[uvwu+w].

a
The critical points lie on the parabolic cylinder v=w2.
b
The critical points lie on the sphere u2+v2+w2=2.
c
The critical points lie on the vw−plane.
d
The critical points lie on the plane u=w.
e
The critical points lie on the uv−plane.
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

For a transformation

T:[uvw]→[x(u,v,w)y(u,v,w)z(u,v,w)],

the Jacobian determinant of T, denoted ∂(x,y,z)∂(u,v,w), is given by

∂(x,y,z)∂(u,v,w)=|∂x∂u∂x∂v∂x∂w∂y∂u∂y∂v∂y∂w∂z∂u∂z∂v∂z∂w|.

Here, we have

x(u,v,w)=u,y(u,v,w)=vw,z(u,v,w)=u+w.

First, we find the partial derivatives:

∂x∂u=12u∂x∂v=0∂x∂w=0∂y∂u=0∂y∂v=w∂y∂w=v∂z∂u=1∂z∂v=0∂z∂w=1

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

∂(x,y,z)∂(u,v,w)=|12u000wv101|=12u|wv01|+1|00wv|=12u(w−0)+0=w2u.

The function has critical points when ∂(x,y,z)∂(u,v,w)=0. So, we obtain

∂(x,y,z)∂(u,v,w)=0w2u=0w=0.

The equation w=0 defines the plane w=0, i.e., uv-plane.

q-161817.name: Question 10
q-161817.problem:
Find the locations of all of the critical points of the transformation $T,$ where $T$ is defined as

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v \\ w\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}u \\ v{e}^{w} \\ 2u+v+3w\end{aligned}].
$$
q-161817.worked_solution:
For a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v \\ w\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have 

$$
x(u,v,w)=u,\,y(u,v,w)=v{e}^{w},\,z(u,v,w)=2u+v+3w.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =1 & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =0 & \,\frac{∂x}{∂w} & =0 \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =0 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & ={e}^{w} & \,\frac{∂y}{∂w} & =v{e}^{w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & =2 & \,\frac{∂z}{∂v} & =1 & \,\frac{∂z}{∂w} & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & {e}^{w} & v{e}^{w} \\ 2 & 1 & 3\end{aligned}| \\  & =1|\begin{aligned}{e}^{w} & v{e}^{w} \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}| \\  & =1(3{e}^{w}-v{e}^{w}) \\  & ={e}^{w}(3-v).\end{aligned}
$$

The function has critical points when $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}=0.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =0 \\ {e}^{w}(3-v) & =0 \\ 3-v & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The equation $3-v=0$ defines the plane $v=3.$

q-161804.name: Question 11
q-161804.problem:
Consider the transformation $T:(u,v,w)\to (x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w)).$ The inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}(x,y,z)\to (u(x,y,z),v(x,y,z),w(x,y,z))$ is given by

$$
{T}^{-1}:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}{e}^{x} \\ {e}^{x+y} \\ {e}^{x+y+z}\end{aligned}].
$$

Find the Jacobian determinant of $T.$
q-161804.worked_solution:
For a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v \\ w\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, we're only given ${T}^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)},$ the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}.$

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ using the relation

$$
\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1}.
$$

Here, we have 

$$
u(x,y,z)={e}^{x},\,v(x,y,z)={e}^{x+y},\,w(x,y,z)={e}^{x+y+z}.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & ={e}^{x} & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & =0 & \,\frac{∂u}{∂z} & =0 \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & ={e}^{x+y} & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & ={e}^{x+y} & \,\frac{∂v}{∂z} & =0 \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & ={e}^{x+y+z} & \,\frac{∂w}{∂y} & ={e}^{x+y+z} & \,\frac{∂w}{∂z} & ={e}^{x+y+z}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}{e}^{x} & 0 & 0 \\ {e}^{x+y} & {e}^{x+y} & 0 \\ {e}^{x+y+z} & {e}^{x+y+z} & {e}^{x+y+z}\end{aligned}| \\  & ={e}^{x}|\begin{aligned}{e}^{x+y} & 0 \\ {e}^{x+y+z} & {e}^{x+y+z}\end{aligned}| \\  & ={e}^{x}({e}^{2x+2y+z}-0) \\  & ={e}^{3x+2y+z}.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing down $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)}$ in terms of $u,$ $v,$ and $w,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{3x+2y+z} & ={e}^{x+(x+y)+(x+y+z)} \\  & ={e}^{x}\cdot {e}^{x+y}\cdot {e}^{x+y+z} \\  & =uvw\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & ={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{uvw}\end{aligned}
$$

  • Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of T using the relation ∂(x,y,z)∂(u,v,w)=(∂(u,v,w)∂(x,y,z))−1.

q-39300.name: Question 12
q-39300.problem:
Consider the transformation $T:(u,v,w)\to (x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w)).$ The inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}(x,y,z)\to (u(x,y,z),v(x,y,z),w(x,y,z))$ is given by

$$
{T}^{-1}:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{x} \\ \sqrt{y}+z \\ {y}^{2}\end{aligned}].
$$

Find the Jacobian determinant of $T.$

*Hint: You can assume that $x\ne 0$ and $y>0.$*
q-39300.worked_solution:
For a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v \\ w\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, we're only given ${T}^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)},$ the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}.$

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ using the relation

$$
\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1}.
$$

Here, we have 

$$
u(x,y,z)=\frac{1}{x},\,y(x,y,z)=\sqrt{y}+z,\,z(x,y,z)={y}^{2}.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}} & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & =0 & \,\frac{∂u}{∂z} & =0 \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & =0 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}} & \,\frac{∂v}{∂z} & =1 \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & =0 & \,\frac{∂w}{∂y} & =2y & \,\frac{∂w}{∂z} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}} & 1 \\ 0 & 2y & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}|\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}} & 1 \\ 2y & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =\frac{2y}{{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing down $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)}$ in terms of $u,$ $v,$ and $w,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2y}{{x}^{2}} & =(\frac{1}{x})^{2}\cdot 2\sqrt{{y}^{2}} \\  & ={u}^{2}\cdot 2\sqrt{w} \\  & =2{u}^{2}\sqrt{w}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & ={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2{u}^{2}\sqrt{w}}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

In this case, we're only given ${T}^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)},$ the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}.$

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ using the relation

$$
\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1}.
$$

Here, we have 

$$
u(x,y,z)=xy,\,v(x,y,z)=yz,\,w(x,y,z)=xz.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =y & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & =x & \,\frac{∂u}{∂z} & =0 \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & =0 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =z & \,\frac{∂v}{∂z} & =y \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & =z & \,\frac{∂w}{∂y} & =0 & \,\frac{∂w}{∂z} & =x\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}y & x & 0 \\ 0 & z & y \\ z & 0 & x\end{aligned}| \\  & =y|\begin{aligned}z & y \\ 0 & x\end{aligned}|-x|\begin{aligned}0 & y \\ z & x\end{aligned}| \\  & =y(xz-0)-x(0-yz) \\  & =xyz+xyz \\  & =2xyz.\end{aligned}

$$

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & ={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{uvw}}\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the transformation T:(u,v,w)→(x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w)). The inverse transformation T−1(x,y,z)→(u(x,y,z),v(x,y,z),w(x,y,z)) is given by T−1:[xyz]⟶[xyyzxz].

Find the Jacobian determinant of T.

2uvw

EXPLANATION

T:[uvw]→[x(u,v,w)y(u,v,w)z(u,v,w)],

∂(x,y,z)∂(u,v,w)=|∂x∂u∂x∂v∂x∂w∂y∂u∂y∂v∂y∂w∂z∂u∂z∂v∂z∂w|.

In this case, we're only given T−1. So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of T as follows:

  • First, we compute ∂(u,v,w)∂(x,y,z), the Jacobian determinant of T−1.

  • Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of T using the relation ∂(x,y,z)∂(u,v,w)=(∂(u,v,w)∂(x,y,z))−1.

Here, we have

u(x,y,z)=xy,v(x,y,z)=yz,w(x,y,z)=xz.

First, we find the partial derivatives: ∂u∂x=y∂u∂y=x∂u∂z=0∂v∂x=0∂v∂y=z∂v∂z=y∂w∂x=z∂w∂y=0∂w∂z=x

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant of T−1 is

∂(u,v,w)∂(x,y,z)=|∂u∂x∂u∂y∂u∂z∂v∂x∂v∂y∂v∂z∂w∂x∂w∂y∂w∂z|=|yx00zyz0x|=y|zy0x|−x|0yzx|=y(xz−0)−x(0−yz)=xyz+xyz=2xyz.

Writing down ∂(u,v,w)∂(x,y,z) in terms of u, v, and w, we obtain 2xyz=2(xyz)2=2x2y2z2=2xy(yz)(xz)=2uvw

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

∂(x,y,z)∂(u,v,w)=(∂(u,v,w)∂(x,y,z))−1=12uvw

q-161800.name: Question 15
q-161800.problem:
Find the Jacobian determinant of the transformation $T:(u,v,w)\to (x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w)),$ given that 

$$
u=z-y,\,v=x+z,\,w=-3x.
$$
q-161800.worked_solution:
For a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v \\ w\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, we're only given ${T}^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)},$ the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}.$

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ using the relation

$$
\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1}.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =0 & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & =-1 & \,\frac{∂u}{∂z} & =1 \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & =1 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =0 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂z} & =1 \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & =-3 & \,\frac{∂w}{∂y} & =0 & \,\frac{∂w}{∂z} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}0 & -1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ -3 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =-(-1)|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -3 & 0\end{aligned}|+1|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -3 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =1(0+3)+1(0-0) \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & ={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}
